title: Adjectives vs Adverbs
summary: Find the word being described, then choose: adjectives for nouns and after linking verbs, adverbs for verbs, adjectives, adverbs and participles — plus good/well, real/really and the tricky -ly words.

blocks.text: "She sings beautiful." "The bridge was real old." "I feel badly." All three sound normal in everyday speech, and all three are errors the ACT likes to test. This lesson teaches one simple question that solves almost every adjective–adverb item — **what word is being described?** — and then the special cases the test uses to catch careful students: linking verbs, good/well, real/really, adverbs before participles, -ly words that are really adjectives, and adverbs that do not end in -ly at all.
What this question type tests

Adjective–adverb questions are usage questions in **Conventions of Standard English**, the reporting category that makes up **38–43%** of the 40 scored ACT English questions (together with punctuation and sentence structure). They look like every other ACT English item: a word or phrase is underlined in the essay and you choose among four versions, usually with **NO CHANGE** first. There is often no question stem at all.

You can recognise the type with a **vertical scan** of the choices: they show the same word in different forms — careful / carefully, quick / quickly, good / well, real / really, surprising / surprisingly. As soon as you see that pattern, stop reading for meaning and ask the grammar question below.
Step 1: Find the word being described
Every describing word is attached to another word. Find that word first; its part of speech decides the answer.

rows: a pronoun after a linking verb
a participle used as an adjective (built, designed, known)
a **newly** built school · a **carefully** designed plan

blocks.text: Most adverbs are adjective + **-ly** (slow → slowly, careful → carefully, easy → easily, gentle → gently, basic → basically). But the ending alone is not proof, as you will see in Step 5.

rows: The new model runs quiet and efficient.
Luckily for us, the shop was open late.
The plan was explained in a surprising simple way.

blocks.title: السؤال الذهبي
blocks.text: قبل ما تختار، اسأل: الكلمة دي بتوصف إيه؟ لو بتوصف اسم (noun) يبقى adjective زي careful. لو بتوصف فعل أو صفة أو ظرف تاني يبقى adverb وغالبًا آخره ly زي carefully. مثال: incredibly fast — كلمة incredibly بتوصف fast (صفة)، علشان كده adverb.
Step 2: Linking verbs take adjectives

This is the rule the ACT tests most often. A **linking verb** does not show an action; it connects the subject to a word that describes the **subject**. So the word after it is an **adjective**, not an adverb.

items: Common linking verbs: **be** (is, are, was, were, been), **seem, appear, become, remain, stay, prove, grow, turn**, and the five sense verbs **look, feel, sound, taste, smell**.
**The "is" test:** replace the verb with *is/was*. If the sentence still makes sense, the verb is linking → use an adjective. "The soup tasted ___" → "The soup was salty" ✓ → **salty**.
✓ The room grew **quiet**. ✗ The room grew quietly. (The room became quiet.)
✓ Her plan sounds **reasonable**. ✗ Her plan sounds reasonably.
✓ The milk turned **sour**. ✓ The results proved **accurate**. ✓ The bread smells **fresh**.
✓ I feel **bad** about the mistake. ✗ I feel badly about the mistake. (*Bad* describes how *I* feel. "Feel badly" would describe how your fingers touch things.)

blocks.text: **The same verb can be linking or action.** Ask whether the verb shows something the subject *does* or simply describes the subject's *state*.

rows: The guard looked **angrily** at the crowd. (How did he look at them?)
The doctor felt the patient's arm **gently**.

blocks.text: **Tip:** if the verb is followed by an object or by a preposition such as *at* (looked at, smelled the bag), it is usually an action verb → adverb.
Step 3: good / well, bad / badly, real / really

rows: She did good on the test.
She did **well** on the test. He sings **well**.
After a week in bed, I finally feel **well**.
I feel badly about it (meaning sorry).

blocks.text: Notice that *I feel good* and *I feel well* can both be correct: *good* describes your mood, *well* means you are not ill. The ACT will make the meaning clear from the passage. What it will never accept is **did good**, **played good** or **real good**.
Step 4: Adverbs before participles and adjectives

A participle (built, designed, known, written, painted) can act like an adjective before a noun. The word that describes the participle must be an **adverb**. This is a favourite hard item because the adjective version "sounds" like a list of two adjectives.

items: ✗ a beautiful decorated room → ✓ a **beautifully** decorated room (it was decorated beautifully)
✗ a new built museum → ✓ a **newly** built museum
✗ a careful written report → ✓ a **carefully** written report
✗ a wide read author → ✓ a **widely** read author
✓ a **beautiful, old** house — here both words describe the noun *house*, so two adjectives are correct.
**Test:** put *and* between the two words. "a beautiful and decorated room" means something different → you need the adverb. "a beautiful and old house" works → two adjectives are fine.

blocks.text: Step 5: -ly adjectives and adverbs without -ly
Some words end in -ly but are **adjectives**: they describe nouns and cannot simply describe a verb. You cannot add another -ly to most of them, so you rewrite with **in a … way / manner**.

rows: a **friendly** neighbour · She smiled **in a friendly way**.
a **lonely** road · a **lively** debate · a **likely** result
a **costly** mistake · an **elderly** man · a **timely** warning
He answered timely. → He answered **in a timely manner**.
He behaved cowardly. → He behaved **in a cowardly way**.
a **daily** walk / I walk **daily** · an **early** train / We left **early**

blocks.text: The opposite group: some adverbs have **no -ly** form, or the -ly form means something different. The test uses these to trap students who add -ly to everything.

headers: Careful: the -ly word means something else
rows: *hardly* = almost not (They hardly worked = they did very little)

blocks.title: افعال الإحساس والكلمات اللي آخرها ly
blocks.text: بعد look وfeel وsound وtaste وsmell وseem وbecome بنستخدم صفة: The soup tastes good و I feel bad — مش badly. جرّب تحط is مكان الفعل: لو المعنى ماشي يبقى صفة. وخلي بالك: friendly وlovely وlonely صفات مع إن آخرها ly، فنقول in a friendly way. وhard ظرف من غير ly، أما hardly معناها "بالكاد".
Worked examples
Each example is a sentence from an ACT-style essay. The underlined portion is shown in **bold**.
**Worked example 1 — adverb describing an adjective.** "The new metro line has made the trip across the city **remarkable** short."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) remarkably short
C) remarkable shortly
D) remarkably shortly

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** *Short* describes the noun *trip* (after *made the trip*), so it stays an adjective. *Remarkably* describes the adjective *short* — how short? — so it must be an adverb.
**A** uses the adjective *remarkable* to describe another adjective. **Trap:** two adjectives side by side often sound acceptable in speech.
**C** reverses the forms: *shortly* means *soon*, and *remarkable* still cannot describe it.
**D** keeps *shortly*, which changes the meaning to "soon" and leaves the trip with no describing word. **Trap:** adding -ly to every word.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — linking verb.** "After the long argument, the meeting room grew **silently**, and nobody wanted to speak first."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) silent
C) more silently
D) in silence way

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** *Grew* here means *became*: the room became silent. The "is" test works (the room was silent), so *grew* is a linking verb and needs the adjective **silent**.
**A** treats *grew* as an action, as if the room were growing in a silent manner. **Trap:** the linking-verb trap.
**C** is still an adverb and adds a comparison with nothing to compare.
**D** is not standard English (the idiom would be *in a silent way*, and even that would describe an action, not a state).

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — adverb before a participle.** "Visitors to the old house admire its **careful restored** wooden balconies."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) carefully restored
C) carefully restoring
D) care-restored

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** The balconies were restored carefully, so *carefully* describes the participle *restored*. An adverb is needed.
**A** uses the adjective *careful*, but the balconies are not careful; the restoring was. Use the *and* test: "careful and restored balconies" makes no sense.
**C** changes the participle to *restoring*, which would mean the balconies are doing the restoring.
**D** is an invented compound.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — -ly adjective.** "The shop owner greeted every customer **friendly**, even on the busiest days of the festival."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) friendlily
C) in a friendly manner
D) friendlier

blocks.text: **Answer: C.**

items: **C is correct.** The word describes how he *greeted* (an action), so we need an adverb idea. *Friendly* is an adjective, and it has no normal -ly adverb, so standard English uses **in a friendly manner** (or *in a friendly way*).
**A** uses the adjective to describe a verb. **Trap:** the -ly ending makes *friendly* look like an adverb.
**B** is an extremely rare, awkward form that the ACT does not accept as standard.
**D** is a comparative with nothing to compare (friendlier than whom?).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5 — hard vs hardly.** "The volunteers worked **hardly** all weekend, and by Sunday evening the whole park had been cleaned."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) hard
C) harder
D) more hardly

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** *Hard* is both an adjective and an adverb: they worked **hard** = with great effort. The second clause (the whole park was cleaned) confirms the meaning.
**A** means *almost not at all*, which contradicts the result. **Trap:** the -ly form exists but has a different meaning.
**C** is a comparative with nothing to compare.
**D** combines two errors: *more* + the wrong word.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **Adjective before an adjective:** *incredible fast, surprising large, real good* → the first word must be an adverb (incredibly, surprisingly, really).
**The linking-verb trap:** adverbs after *seem, become, grow, feel, look, sound, taste, smell* → use adjectives (grew quiet, feel bad, sounds reasonable).
**Action or state?** The same verb (look, smell, taste, feel) can be either; check whether the subject is doing something to an object.
**good for well:** did good, played good, sings good → well.
**Adjective before a participle:** *a beautiful decorated hall, a new built bridge* → beautifully, newly.
**The -ly illusion:** friendly, lovely, costly and timely are adjectives; you cannot say *spoke friendly*.
**The meaning-change -ly:** hardly ≠ hard, lately ≠ late, highly ≠ high, nearly ≠ near.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Vertical scan shows careful/carefully, good/well, real/really? Ask: *what word is being described?*
Noun → adjective. Verb, adjective, adverb or participle → adverb.
Verb before the blank is *is, seem, become, look, feel, sound, taste, smell*? Try *is*. If it works, choose the adjective.
Two describing words before a noun? Use the *and* test.
Eliminate any choice that adds a comparison (more, -er) when nothing is being compared.
If the -ly word changes the meaning (hardly, lately), check the sentence's logic.

blocks.text: Practice
Two short ACT-style essays with 5 questions each. The numbers in brackets match the question numbers. Every question tests adjectives and adverbs.

blocks.title: Adjectives vs Adverbs — ACT-style practice
blocks.intro: Two ACT-style essays, 10 questions. Choose the best version of each underlined portion; NO CHANGE keeps the original. Explanations appear after you answer.

questions.p:
The Lantern Maker

Every year, a few weeks before Ramadan, the workshop of Hajj Saber fills with the sound of hammers. For more than forty years he has made fanous lanterns by hand, and his small shop in Old Cairo has become __real famous__ [1] among collectors.

Saber works __slow and patient__ [2]. He cuts each sheet of tin with heavy scissors, bends it into shape and joins the edges with a flame no larger than a candle's. Visitors who watch him are often surprised by how __quiet__ [3] the old craftsman seems while he works. He hums to himself but rarely speaks.

The finished lanterns are __beautiful decorated__ [4] with pieces of red, green and blue glass. When a candle is lit inside, the glass throws coloured patterns across the walls of the shop. Saber admits that a lantern made by a machine may look __good__ [5] on a shelf, but he insists that it will never glow the way a handmade one does. His customers seem to agree: by the first night of Ramadan, almost every shelf in the workshop is empty.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: *Famous* is an adjective, so the word that describes it must be an adverb: **really** (= very). *Real* (A) is an adjective meaning *genuine* and cannot describe another adjective. C and D are not standard forms.

questions.q: [5] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: Here *look* is a linking verb: the lantern *is* good (in appearance). Linking verbs take adjectives, so **good** is correct. *Well* (B) as an adjective means *healthy*, which does not fit a lantern; C is not modern standard English; D is an adverb after a linking verb.

questions.p:
The Fennec Fox

The fennec fox is the smallest fox in the world, but its ears are __surprising large__ [6]. They can grow up to fifteen centimetres long, and they help the animal hear insects moving under the sand. The ears also release body heat, which keeps the fox cool during the desert summer.

Fennecs spend the hottest hours of the day in burrows, which they dig __quick__ [7] with their strong front paws. At night they work __hardly__ [8], sometimes travelling several kilometres in search of insects, lizards and seeds. Their thick fur protects them when the desert temperature drops __sharp__ [9] after sunset.

In the wild, fennecs are shy and avoid people. In zoos, however, many of them learn to behave __friendly__ [10] toward the keepers who feed them, and some will even take food from a keeper's hand.
questions.q: [6] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: *Large* is an adjective describing the ears; the word that describes *large* must be the adverb **surprisingly**. A puts an adjective before an adjective; C and D use the wrong word forms.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Find the word being described: noun → adjective; verb, adjective, adverb or participle → adverb.
Linking verbs (be, seem, become, grow, look, feel, sound, taste, smell) take adjectives: feel bad, look good, grew quiet.
good = adjective; well = adverb (or *healthy*); real = genuine; really = very.
friendly, lovely, costly are adjectives → *in a friendly way*.
hard, fast, late, high are adverbs too — and hardly, lately, highly mean something else.
